web_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: The Forensic Ledger — 10-Year P&L, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet Reality
question: What does a 10-year forensic audit of AMD's GAAP vs. Non-GAAP earnings, cash flow conversion, ROIC, goodwill overhang, debt, and share dilution reveal about its true economic quality?

epigraph.quote: Revenue is vanity, Non-GAAP profit is opinion, and Free Cash Flow after real dilution is sanity.
epigraph.author: Forensic accounting maxim

web_blocks.html: Ten years of audited SEC filings show rapid secular growth paired with sharp profit swings [1][2][5]. From FY2016 to FY2025, revenue grew 8.0x from $4,319 million to $34,639 million (26.0% CAGR) [1][5]. Nine-month 2026 revenue of $35,166 million already topped all of FY2025 [2]. GAAP gross margin climbed from 23.2% in FY2016 to 49.5% in FY2025 and 53.5% in 9M 2026 [1][2][5]. Yet GAAP operating income swung wildly: from $(373) million in FY2016 to $3,648 million in FY2021, down 89% to $401 million in FY2023, and back up to $3,694 million in FY2025 and $6,298 million in 9M 2026 [1][2][5].

web_blocks.caption: AMD 10-Year Audited Financial Summary & 9M 2026 Update ($ Millions, Except % and Shares)
web_blocks.takeaway: *FY2025 consolidated CFO was $7,709M (including $1,216M from discontinued ZT Manufacturing); continuing-operations CFO was $6,493M and continuing-operations FCF was $5,519M ($6,493M minus $974M CapEx) [1]. 9M 2026 continuing-ops FCF reached $4,678M despite massive working-capital absorption [2].

web_blocks.html: Notice how fixed R&D and acquisition amortization dictate earnings volatility across this ten-year ledger [1][5]. Even a 3.9% sales dip in FY2023 cut GAAP operating income by 89%, whereas 2026's 44% sales surge drove GAAP operating profit up more than threefold YoY [1][2].

web_blocks.title: 6.2 Forensic GAAP vs. Non-GAAP Bridge: What Is Real vs. What Is Cosmetic?

web_blocks.html: Forensic analysis must unpack the wide gap between GAAP and Non-GAAP profits. In FY2025, GAAP operating income was $3,694 million (10.7% margin) versus Non-GAAP operating income of $7,768 million (22.4% margin) [1][4]. That $4,074 million gap splits into two very different buckets [1][4].

1. Non-Cash Acquisition Amortization ($2,254M in FY2025; $1,629M in 9M 2026): Mostly tied to the 2022 Xilinx purchase, this non-cash charge does not drain cash [1][2]. It steps down from $2,153 million in FY2026 to $1,454 million in FY2030 before World Labs and Taalas intangibles are added [1]. Adding it back to gauge operating cash power is fair. 2. Real Economic Dilution — Stock-Based Pay ($1,638M in FY2025; $1,513M in 9M 2026): SBC is a real recurring payroll cost equal to 4.7% of FY2025 sales and 29.7% of continuing-ops FCF [1][2]. In 9M 2026, AMD also booked a $1,179 million non-cash customer warrant charge for OpenAI and Meta under ASC 606/718 [2]. True owner earnings therefore sit between GAAP and Non-GAAP: add back amortization, but treat SBC and warrants as real costs.

web_blocks.title: 6.3 Cash Conversion, Working Capital Drag & CapEx Inflection

web_blocks.html: Cash conversion is strong over full cycles but tightens during major product ramps. In FY2025, continuing-ops CFO hit $6,493 million (152.1% of continuing-ops net income), yielding $5,519 million in FCF (15.9% margin; 11.2% ex-SBC) [1]. Note that FY2025 GAAP net income also got a $853 million one-time IRS tax reserve release and $366 million in investment gains [1]. In 9M 2026, Helios scaling absorbed heavy working capital: receivables used $2,894 million, inventories used $3,543 million, and prepaids used $2,061 million, partly offset by $4,483 million in payables [2]. Nine-month CFO reached $6,523 million (106.8% of net income), while CapEx more than doubled to $1,845 million, leaving $4,678 million in FCF (13.3% margin; 9.0% ex-SBC) [2].

web_blocks.title: 6.4 Balance Sheet, Goodwill Overhang, ROIC & Dilution Forensics

web_blocks.html: At September 26, 2026, AMD held $15,776 million in cash and short-term investments ($7,404 million cash plus $8,372 million investments) [2]. Against $7,079 million in net long-term debt (after August 2026's $4.75 billion bond issue), AMD holds +$8,697 million in net cash plus an undrawn $5.0 billion revolver [2]. Yet three forensic factors qualify that liquid cushion.

First, Goodwill ($25,470M) and Intangibles ($15,101M) totaled $40,571 million at Q3 2026—42.8% of total assets and 59.3% of equity [2]. Closing World Labs (~$8.2 billion) and Taalas (~$2.9 billion) in November 2026 will push goodwill and intangibles past ~$50 billion [2][11][12]. That heavy base depressed FY2025 GAAP ROIC to roughly 5.6% (below ~9%–10% WACC) [1]. Excluding Xilinx goodwill and intangibles, organic tangible ROIC exceeds 22%, proving the core silicon business earns high returns while M&A premiums dilute consolidated capital efficiency [1].

Second, Share Dilution Risk Has Risen Sharply. From FY2022 to FY2025, steady buybacks ($6.86 billion total) kept diluted shares flat near 1,636 million [1][5]. In 9M 2026, open-market buybacks fell to just $221 million (with $1,836 million spent on employee tax withholdings), and diluted shares rose to 1,661 million in Q3 2026 [2]. Looking ahead, AMD faces 320 million customer warrant shares (~19.3% potential dilution) plus all-stock World Labs and partial-stock Taalas issuances [2][6][7][10]. Third, AMD's $8.70 billion net cash cushion sits beneath $81.8 billion in off-balance-sheet purchase, lease, guarantee, and equity pledges [2].

book_paragraphs: Now you and I open the forensic ledger—ten full years of audited SEC numbers from 2016 through the third quarter of 2026. The first thing that jumps off the page is sheer scale: AMD's annual revenue multiplied eightfold from 4.3 billion dollars in 2016 to 34.6 billion dollars in 2025, and in the first nine months of 2026 alone AMD already booked 35.2 billion dollars. GAAP gross margin climbed more than thirty percentage points over that decade, from 23.2 percent to 53.5 percent.

Yet the second thing a forensic reader notices is just how violently profits swing when semiconductor cycles turn—and how wide the gap has become between GAAP accounting and Non-GAAP press releases. In FY2025, AMD reported 3.69 billion dollars in GAAP operating profit versus 7.77 billion dollars in Non-GAAP operating profit—a four-billion-dollar chasm. Never accept Non-GAAP blindly, and never accept GAAP blindly either. Break the gap into its two real pieces.

Piece one is 2.25 billion dollars in annual non-cash amortization of acquired intangibles, mostly left over from the 49-billion-dollar Xilinx deal. That money left the building in 2022; adding it back to judge ongoing cash earning power makes total sense. Piece two is 1.64 billion dollars in annual stock-based compensation—and 1.51 billion dollars already in the first nine months of 2026—plus 1.18 billion dollars in non-cash customer warrant accounting charges from the OpenAI and Meta deals. Those are NOT bookkeeping ghosts. Paying engineers and hyperscaler customers in AMD shares is a real economic cost borne directly by existing shareholders.

book_subsections.title: Cash Conversion, ROIC & The Goodwill Hangover
paragraphs: Look next at cash flow quality. In FY2025, continuing-operations operating cash flow hit 6.49 billion dollars and Free Cash Flow reached 5.52 billion dollars—15.9 percent of revenue, or 11.2 percent after deducting stock-based pay. In the first nine months of 2026, however, ramping Helios and MI450 sucked cash into the supply chain: receivables and inventories together absorbed 6.44 billion dollars, and capital spending more than doubled to 1.85 billion dollars, keeping nine-month Free Cash Flow at 4.68 billion dollars (13.3 percent of sales).

Then examine Return on Invested Capital. Because 40.6 billion dollars of Xilinx goodwill and intangibles sit on AMD's balance sheet—a figure set to top 50 billion dollars once November 2026's World Labs and Taalas acquisitions hit the books—headline GAAP ROIC in FY2025 sat near 5.6 percent, below AMD's cost of capital. Strip out that historical acquisition goodwill, and AMD's organic silicon engine earns well over 22 percent on tangible operating capital. The message is crystal clear: AMD's core chip engineering is a high-return machine, yet management's appetite for multi-billion-dollar stock acquisitions has repeatedly diluted consolidated return on capital.

book_subsections.title: Decoding the OpenAI & Meta Warrants in the Accounting Footnotes
paragraphs: Most retail investors skim press releases and celebrate gigawatt headlines; forensic analysts read Note 2 and Note 11 of the Form 10-Q. Under U.S. accounting rules (ASC 606 and ASC 718), warrants granted to a customer are not free marketing tokens—they are treated as consideration payable to a customer. That means the grant-date fair value of the OpenAI and Meta warrants is recorded as a reduction to revenue proportionally as qualifying Instinct GPUs ship, while subsequent fair-value remeasurements swing through Other Income and Expense until each tranche vests.

In the first nine months of 2026 alone, the cash flow statement reveals a 1.18-billion-dollar non-cash impact from warrants issued to customers. If OpenAI and Meta fulfill all six gigawatts each and meet all vesting conditions, AMD would issue up to 320 million new shares at one penny apiece—diluting existing shareholders by nearly 19.3 percent on top of the 8.2 billion dollars in stock issued for World Labs and roughly 1.6 billion dollars a year in employee stock-based compensation. That is not necessarily a bad trade if those 12 gigawatts generate hundreds of billions in high-margin revenue—but you must account for that future share count when judging per-share compounding power.

book_subsections.title: Debt, Buybacks, and the True Owner Earnings Test
paragraphs: Finally, trace how AMD's capital allocation shifted in 2026. Between 2022 and 2025, AMD behaved like a classic cash-rich fabless compounder, repurchasing over 6.8 billion dollars of stock to keep its diluted share count flat around 1.63 billion shares. In 2026, management pivoted into full offensive expansion: issuing 4.75 billion dollars in senior notes in August, expanding its revolving credit line to 5.0 billion dollars, slowing open-market buybacks to just 221 million dollars across nine months, and committing 5.1 billion dollars to private AI equity investments plus 1.0 billion dollars to a public equity stake in October 2026.

When we strip away accounting noise and ask what true owner earnings look like today, we see a powerful dual reality. On a nine-month 2026 run rate, AMD is generating over 6.2 billion dollars in annualized Free Cash Flow even while funding 6.4 billion dollars of working capital build and 2.5 billion dollars of annualized CapEx. Once Helios working capital normalizes, cash generation could surge dramatically. Until then, however, elevated stock dilution, goodwill above 50 billion dollars post-World Labs, and 81.8 billion dollars of off-balance-sheet commitments keep AMD firmly in the high-upside, high-conditionality camp.

book_subsections.title: Fortress Liquidity vs. Future Dilution
paragraphs: On its face, AMD's balance sheet at September 26, 2026 looks sturdy: 15.78 billion dollars in cash and short-term investments against 7.08 billion dollars in long-term debt (after issuing 4.75 billion dollars in senior notes in August 2026), leaving 8.70 billion dollars in net cash. Yet as a careful owner, you have to put three items side by side: 8.70 billion dollars of net cash on the balance sheet, 81.8 billion dollars of off-balance-sheet purchase, lease, guarantee, and equity obligations in Note 11, and a looming dilution wave from 320 million OpenAI and Meta warrant shares plus 8.2 billion dollars in stock for World Labs—all while open-market share buybacks slowed to a trickle of 221 million dollars in the first nine months of 2026.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: Here is our price-blind verdict after six chapters of pure business forensics. AMD is no longer a fragile turnaround—it is a world-class engineering franchise with a fortress in EPYC server CPUs, a recovering 40-percent-margin Embedded crown jewel, and genuine hyperscaler traction in Helios AI racks. Yet we cannot honestly call it a low-risk, steady-state compounder. Its profits remain deeply cyclical across semiconductor waves, and its 2026 leap into 81.8 billion dollars of off-balance-sheet obligations, 320 million customer warrant shares, and 11.1 billion dollars of pre-revenue AI acquisitions makes its business quality strictly CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL—with strong current KPIs that demand disciplined risk monitoring.
